directions.name: Parchment and Ink
directions.summary: Warm paper and a bitter-brown ink: quiet, material and typographic.
directions.curation: Built on the printed page: one paper stock and one ink. A neutral pair leaves the color to food, rooms and photography.

reasoning.claim: Bitter Brown reaches {ratio:figure/ground} on Warm Paper, enough for long menus and reading.
A paper-and-ink pair reads as material rather than decorative, so plates, rooms and photography supply the color.

directions.watch_out: Can feel too restrained if the room is also very quiet. Add character through type, not extra colors.
directions.choose_if: the brand should feel typographic and quiet, with photography or the product carrying the color
do: Build hierarchy with weight and size.
avoid: Do not add gold to make it feel premium.

directions.name: Lacquer Room
directions.summary: A lacquer-black ground with cinnabar red: evening drama without gold.
directions.curation: Drawn from lacquerware, black with a cinnabar figure, as a dark premium option that does not lean on gold.

reasoning.claim: Cinnabar reaches {ratio:figure/ground} on Lacquer Black, so it is kept to display type, the mark and dividers.
Red on black gives evening atmosphere and strong hierarchy, and avoids the gold-on-black habit of premium dining.

directions.watch_out: Cinnabar turns loud if it fills large areas. Keep it to about an eighth of the page.
directions.choose_if: the venue or product is evening-focused and should feel dark and dramatic without gold
do: Use Cinnabar as a line, a mark or a single headline.
avoid: Do not set body text in Cinnabar.

directions.name: Clay and Linen
directions.summary: Linen with a muted rose clay: soft, earthy and easy beside food photography.
directions.curation: A soft earth pair for brands that lead with photography. The clay is rosier and quieter than the common terracotta.

reasoning.claim: Rose Clay reaches {ratio:figure/ground} on Linen, so it can carry headings and links.
Low-chroma earth tones sit beside food photography without competing with it.

directions.watch_out: Contrast is moderate, so keep long body copy in the derived text color and check small type.
directions.choose_if: food or product photography leads and the palette should stay soft and warm
do: Pair it with warm, natural-light photography.
avoid: Do not push the clay toward orange terracotta, the most overused version of this pairing.

directions.name: Porcelain and Indigo
directions.summary: Warm porcelain white with a deep indigo: precise, cool and contemporary.
directions.curation: Taken from blue-and-white porcelain: a cool figure on a warm white, as a precise alternative to warm or dark palettes.

reasoning.claim: Indigo reaches {ratio:figure/ground} on Porcelain, so one color carries headings, links and the button.
A cool figure steps away from the warm, gold-leaning language that is common in fine dining.

use_for: Brands that want to feel precise and modern
Websites with a lot of white space
directions.watch_out: Easy to under-use. Indigo needs real presence, such as the mark and every heading.
directions.choose_if: the brand should feel precise and modern, and step away from warm or gold category colors
do: Give Indigo the mark and all headings.
avoid: Do not add a second strong color.

directions.name: Oxblood and Pistachio
directions.summary: Two confident flat fields, oxblood and pistachio, for a contemporary concept.
directions.curation: A bold contemporary option built as two flat fields, for restaurants with a strong concept.

reasoning.claim: Pistachio reaches {ratio:figure/ground} on Oxblood, so either color can carry type on the other.
Two strong colors in large blocks feel confident and contemporary, which suits a concept-led restaurant more than a classic one.

directions.watch_out: At 60/40 there is no quiet field, so photography needs neutral breathing room around it.
directions.choose_if: the concept is bold and contemporary and can carry two strong colors in large blocks
do: Compose in large flat fields with hard edges.
avoid: Do not add a third strong color.

directions.name: Espresso and Milk
directions.summary: Espresso brown and steamed-milk white, with a small caramel accent.
directions.curation: The colors of the product itself, kept neutral so packaging and photography stay readable.

reasoning.claim: Steamed Milk reaches {ratio:figure/ground} on Espresso, so the dark ground can carry everything.
Caramel holds 4% of the declared area, so it works as a signal rather than a theme.

directions.watch_out: Brown grounds look muddy in poor print. Test the espresso on the actual stock.
directions.choose_if: the brand is a cafe or coffee product and should look like the product itself
do: Use Caramel for prices, tags and one action.
avoid: Do not use Caramel for text on Espresso at small sizes.

directions.name: Matcha Field
directions.summary: One green family from pale matcha powder to the deep leaf.
directions.curation: A single hue family built from the product, with variation only in lightness, so the identity is the tea itself.

reasoning.claim: Deep Matcha reaches {ratio:figure/ground} on Matcha Mist, so a one-hue system still reads clearly.
One hue family feels focused and specific to the product rather than generically natural.

directions.watch_out: A single hue family can look flat in large layouts. Use the derived tints for surfaces.
directions.choose_if: there is a single hero product whose own color should define the identity
do: Use tints for panels and shades for type.
avoid: Do not add a second hue.
